prompt.context: Our client is a supplier to the microwavable popcorn industry. They supply popcorn makers (e.g., Act II, Orville Redenbacher's) with the grease-resistant paper used to package popcorn kernels in a variety of serving sizes. In this industry, the quality of the paper is determined by placing a bag of freshly microwaved popcorn on a napkin and measuring the amount of grease that seeps through the paper packaging and is absorbed by the napkin. The R&D department of our client recently developed a new type of paper that doubles the performance of the paper. A new type of coating is applied to the paper that virtually eliminates any seepage of grease in the napkin test.
prompt.question: Should our client introduce this new product into the market?

clarifying_info.q: What is the overall market size?
clarifying_info.a: Overall volume in the market is 100 million sheets of grease-resistant paper per year.

There are 4 players who supply paper in this market. Our client holds the largest market share (50%), with the rest of market share split evenly among the 3 competitors. Market share for all players has been stable over the last decade.

clarifying_info.q: How did our client achieve the larger market share?
clarifying_info.a: They were the first mover into the market.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any difference between the paper supplied by our client and competitors?
clarifying_info.a: All players have been producing and supplying essentially the same type and quality of paper since microwavable popcorn was introduced.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a history of innovations in the grease-resistant paper market?
clarifying_info.a: All players have been producing and supplying essentially the same type and quality of paper since microwavable popcorn was introduced.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any threat of the popcorn makers vertically integrating?
clarifying_info.a: Not really; popcorn makers differentiate on brand and are not really interested in entering production of what is essentially a commodity product.

clarifying_info.q: Is there pricing pressure in this market?
clarifying_info.a: Prices have been relatively stable over the last decade, though recently there has been some increasing pressure as the retail price for microwavable popcorn has been dropping.

clarifying_info.q: Will our client's customers be able to differentiate themselves by using the new paper?
clarifying_info.a: They have not had direct conversations with the popcorn makers. Initial focus groups with end-customers (buyers of popcorn) found that the amount of grease that seeps through paper is not a concern for buyers, and introducing the new paper will not necessarily sway consumers' buying decisions.

clarifying_info.q: Will producing the new paper require a large capital investment?
clarifying_info.a: The cost of setting up the new production will be minimal.

clarifying_info.q: Will the new paper increase our client's raw material costs?
clarifying_info.a: It currently costs our client $0.10 to produce each sheet of paper. The chemicals in the coating of the new paper increase the cost of a sheet by 20% to $0.12.

clarifying_info.q: Will our client's customers incur any additional costs to accommodate the new paper?
clarifying_info.a: They will not incur any extra costs in the production/packaging process. In fact, they will actually save money. The old paper required popcorn makers to glue two sheets together before packaging in order to achieve the desired grease resistance, adding $0.12 to their packaging costs. The new paper allows popcorn makers to eliminate this step. See packaging cost table: Old process: 2 sheets at $0.20 each + $0.12 gluing = $0.52 total. New process: 1 sheet at unknown price + $0.00 gluing = unknown total.

framework: Understand the supply chain: client supplies grease-resistant paper to popcorn makers, who sell to end consumers; innovations must create value at each link
Assess end-consumer demand: does the improvement matter to retail buyers of popcorn?
Analyze volume impact: switching from 2-sheet to 1-sheet packaging halves volume sold to each popcorn maker
Determine cost impact for client: new coating raises production cost from $0.10 to $0.12 per sheet (+20%)
Determine cost impact for popcorn makers: analyze old vs. new total packaging cost to find acceptable price range
Develop pricing strategy: find a price that maintains or grows client profitability while lowering total packaging costs for popcorn makers
Consider competitive and strategic implications: patent protection, pre-selling to customers, market share capture

questions.prompt: What happens to the volume our client sells if popcorn makers switch to the new paper?
questions.guidance: Popcorn makers currently glue 2 sheets together per package. The new paper achieves the same grease resistance with 1 sheet, so the number of sheets purchased per package drops from 2 to 1 — a 50% reduction in volume. With stable market share the client's total unit volume would drop by 50% (from 50 million sheets to 25 million sheets).

math.setup: Client current volume = 100M market × 50% share = 50M sheets. New paper requires 1 sheet per package instead of 2, so volume sold drops to 25M sheets.
steps: New paper: 1 sheet replaces 2 sheets → client volume = 50M / 2 = 25M sheets/year
math.answer: Client volume drops from 50M to 25M sheets per year — a 50% decline

questions.prompt: What price should our client charge for the new paper to maintain its current profitability?
questions.guidance: Calculate current profit, then find the price P for the new paper such that profit at 25M sheets equals current profit at 50M sheets. Current revenue = 50M × $0.20 = $10M; current cost = 50M × $0.10 = $5M; current profit = $5M. New profit equation: (P - $0.12) × 25M = $5M → P = $0.32. But the candidate must also check whether popcorn makers would accept P = $0.32 — compare total packaging costs old vs. new.

math.setup: Current: price = $0.20/sheet, cost = $0.10/sheet, volume = 50M sheets. New: cost = $0.12/sheet, volume = 25M sheets. Solve for P such that profit is unchanged.
math.answer: Client must charge $0.32 per sheet of new paper to maintain current profitability

questions.prompt: Would popcorn makers accept a price of $0.32 per sheet? What is the acceptable price range?
questions.guidance: Compare total packaging costs under old and new processes. Old: 2 sheets × $0.20 + $0.12 gluing = $0.52. New at $0.32: 1 sheet × $0.32 + $0.00 = $0.32 — a significant saving. Any price below $0.52 is acceptable to popcorn makers (they pay less than before). The optimal range that benefits both parties is $0.32 (floor — client breaks even) to just under $0.52 (ceiling — popcorn makers break even). Charging below $0.52 lowers their packaging costs, which is attractive given increasing retail pricing pressure. A superior answer recommends a price in the range ($0.32, $0.52) that shares the savings and could be used to capture market share from competitors.

math.setup: Old total packaging cost for popcorn makers: 2 sheets × $0.20 + $0.12 glue. New total cost: 1 sheet × P_new + $0.00.
steps: New total at P = $0.52: 1 × $0.52 = $0.52 (popcorn maker neutral)
New total at P = $0.32: 1 × $0.32 = $0.32 (popcorn maker saves $0.20)
Client profit at P = $0.52: (0.52 - 0.12) × 25M = 0.40 × 25M = $10M (doubles current profit)
Client profit at P = $0.32: (0.32 - 0.12) × 25M = 0.20 × 25M = $5M (matches current profit)
math.answer: Acceptable price range: $0.32 (client break-even) to $0.52 (popcorn maker break-even). Any price in this range is mutually beneficial. At $0.52 client doubles profit; at $0.32 client maintains current profit and popcorn maker saves $0.20 per package.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional steps should our client take to capitalize on this opportunity?

categories.name: Intellectual Property Protection
ideas: File patents on the new coating formula and manufacturing process
Explore trade secret protection for proprietary coating chemistry

categories.name: Customer Development
ideas: Conduct direct conversations with popcorn makers to validate interest and acceptable price points
Pre-sell the innovation to key accounts before full launch
Offer pilots or trials to demonstrate cost savings

categories.name: Pricing and Go-to-Market
ideas: Set price in the range $0.32–$0.52 to share cost savings with popcorn makers
Use cost-saving narrative (vs. new product pitch) to overcome sticker shock on higher per-sheet price
Consider tiered pricing or volume discounts to win share from competitors

categories.name: Competitive Strategy
ideas: Move quickly before competitors can replicate the innovation
Leverage first-mover advantage and existing 50% market share to lock in contracts
Monitor whether competitors respond with similar coating technology

categories.name: Sales and Marketing
ideas: Arm sales team with total-cost-of-ownership comparisons
Target accounts under the most retail pricing pressure first

recommendation: Our client should introduce the new paper at a price between $0.32 and $0.52 per sheet

At any price in this range, both the client and its popcorn-maker customers benefit: popcorn makers reduce total packaging costs (important given increasing retail price pressure), while the client maintains or significantly increases profitability despite a 50% volume decline
The rationale for introduction is cost reduction for popcorn makers, not end-consumer demand creation — this framing should drive the sales pitch
risks: Popcorn makers may resist what they perceive as a large per-sheet price increase (from $0.20 to $0.32+) without understanding the total-cost savings
Competitors could replicate the coating technology if it is not patent-protected
If the new paper is not adopted broadly, the client risks incurring higher unit costs ($0.12 vs. $0.10) with no revenue upside
next_steps: Secure patent or trade-secret protection on the new coating immediately
Initiate direct conversations with popcorn makers, leading with a total-cost-of-ownership analysis
Develop a pre-sales program with key accounts to build adoption before a full market launch
Determine optimal price point within the $0.32–$0.52 range based on customer negotiations and competitive dynamics
